title: Handling outdated documentation debt: a guide for technical writers on Mac
metaTitle: Handling outdated documentation debt: a guide for technical writers on Mac
description: Learn how to manage documentation debt through systematic content auditing. Practical steps for technical writers to maintain accuracy without burnout.
intro: Handling outdated documentation debt requires a shift from manual, document by document reviews to a data driven, systematic audit process. Technical writers often struggle with the sheer volume of stale content that accumulates as products evolve, leading to significant time loss and professional burnout.
tldr: Prioritize audits based on usage data like page views and support ticket trends.
Use a standardized rubric to evaluate content accuracy and relevance objectively.
Adopt topic based authoring to reduce the amount of content needing manual updates.
Schedule regular, small audit cycles instead of massive annual projects.
Leverage tools like Screaming Frog on your Mac to identify broken links and structural issues.

blocks.text: Why technical documentation audit processes fail

Most documentation debt grows because audits are treated as rare, massive projects. When you wait a year to review hundreds of pages, the task becomes overwhelming. This creates intense, short term pressure that is a known driver of professional burnout. Many writers attempt to audit everything at once, which is unsustainable.

Manual reviews are also prone to subjectivity. Without a clear rubric, it is easy to focus on minor style issues while missing critical accuracy gaps. When you do not have data to show which pages users actually visit, you end up spending hours updating documentation that nobody reads.
The cost of ignored documentation debt

Ignoring outdated content leads to a direct increase in support tickets. Users cannot find the right information, so they reach out to your team. This forces you to spend more time answering repetitive questions instead of writing new material. It creates a cycle where you have even less time for maintenance, and the debt grows further.

items: Prioritize by traffic: Check your analytics to see which pages have the most views. Audit these first.
Check support tickets: If a specific feature triggers many support requests, that documentation is likely unclear or outdated.
Create a rubric: Define what 'good' looks like before you start. Use criteria like factual accuracy, link health, and style guide compliance.
Use crawlers: Tools like Screaming Frog SEO Spider can crawl your documentation site to find broken links and missing metadata instantly.
Adopt topic based authoring: By breaking content into smaller, reusable components, you only need to update a single topic when a feature changes, rather than editing dozens of pages.

blocks.text: Using your Mac to support your audit workflow

You can use your Mac to automate the data gathering part of your audit. Keep your audit rubric in a Notion database or a Google Sheet. Use your browser to export traffic data from your documentation platform. If you use a static site generator, you can run build scripts in your terminal to check for broken links as part of your daily routine.
How Lazur helps with documentation maintenance

Lazur helps you manage the administrative burden of auditing. You can use it to quickly draft emails to subject matter experts to verify technical details. When you are reviewing a long page, you can ask Lazur to summarize the key points to help you identify missing information or outdated sections.

faq.question: How often should I conduct a documentation audit?
faq.answer: Instead of one large annual audit, try a continuous model. Review a small set of pages every week based on user feedback or analytics.

faq.question: What tools can I use on a Mac for auditing?
faq.answer: You can use Screaming Frog SEO Spider for link checking, Notion or Google Sheets for tracking your audit progress, and your browser analytics tools to identify high traffic pages.

faq.question: Does Lazur automate the content audit for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not crawl your site or edit files. It helps you by summarizing notes, drafting communications with SMEs, and guiding you through your own manual review process.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Review analytics
plan.text: Spend 30 minutes identifying the top 10 most visited pages that have not been updated in six months.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Audit first batch
plan.text: Audit the first three pages from your list using your rubric. Check for broken links and factual accuracy.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: SME outreach
plan.text: Ask Lazur to draft emails to SMEs about the issues you found in Tuesday's audit.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Implement fixes
plan.text: Update the content based on the feedback you received. Use your documentation tool's style guide.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Final check
plan.text: Run a final link check on the updated pages and document your progress in your tracker.
